text: Comparing a query vector to every single stored vector works fine for a few thousand vectors, but it doesn't scale. An index is a structure built ahead of time that lets a query skip most of those comparisons.

A brute-force scan is exact but its cost grows directly with collection size — a million vectors means a million comparisons, every query. That's why real vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbor search instead: a small, tunable amount of accuracy traded for a very large amount of speed.

Here's IVF in numbers. A million vectors, split into a thousand clusters, puts roughly a thousand vectors in each one. A query compares against the thousand cluster centroids first, then probes only the ten closest clusters — scanning about ten thousand vectors instead of a million. That's a hundred times fewer comparisons.

IVF clusters the vector space at build time, using something like k-means to produce those centroids. At query time it probes only the nearest few. And nprobe is the tuning knob — probe more clusters for better recall, fewer for more speed.

HNSW takes a completely different approach — a layered graph instead of clusters. The top layer has just a handful of nodes connected by long jumps across the space. Each layer down gets denser, until the bottom layer holds every single vector, locally linked to its neighbors.

A search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily moves toward whichever connected node is closest to the query, descending a layer each time it can't get any closer. The ef parameter controls how many candidates stay in play at each step — higher ef means better recall, at the cost of speed.

Most vector databases default to HNSW for its recall at speed, while IVF trades some of that for a smaller memory footprint at massive scale. Next lesson: metadata filtering, narrowing a search by more than just vector similarity.
